company.name: HFCL
company.summary: HFCL makes the glass fibre cables that carry internet data, plus telecom equipment and defence electronics.
company.description: Phone calls, video, cloud services and AI programs all reach you as pulses of light along hair-thin strands of glass called optical fibre. HFCL makes that fibre, wraps many strands into protected cables, and makes the equipment at the ends of the network, such as Wi-Fi systems, routers and radio links. Its customers are phone companies, very large technology companies that run data centres, governments and armed forces. It also makes defence electronics such as thermal sights and radars, and builds telecom networks to order. Its factories are in Hyderabad, Goa, Chennai and Hosur.
company.ownership: This profile covers HFCL Limited, formerly Himachal Futuristic Communications Limited, and its subsidiary HTL Limited. It makes cables and equipment and builds networks for customers; it is not a mobile phone company and does not sell broadband to households. A proposed purchase of an aerospace business was announced but is described by the company as proposed, not completed.
products: Hair-thin glass strands that carry data as light
Fibre bundled and protected for laying underground or on poles
Cabling and connectors inside large computer buildings
Equipment that sends data through the air and between networks
Wireless links that carry mobile-tower traffic to the main network
Radars that detect movement over ground or sea
Cable assemblies for defence, aerospace and cars
Designing and installing telecom networks to order
company.money: HFCL earns money when customers pay for the cables and equipment it ships, and for network-building work under contract. Its costs are the glass and plastic materials for fibre and cable, factory running costs, engineers and research, and interest on loans. Large orders take months to make and deliver, so HFCL spends before it is paid.
watch: How dependent is HFCL on a few very large customers?
Sales that rely on a few customers can swing sharply if one changes its plans.
Are orders turning into delivered goods and cash?
An order book only helps if it is delivered and paid for.
Are the new factories ready and will they be used?
Extra capacity costs money before it earns any.
Is defence turning into reliable earnings?
Defence orders can be large but irregular and slow to be approved and paid.
Do profit margins hold when growth settles?
A very strong quarter after a weak one may not repeat.
risks: A big customer cuts back or changes supplier
A small number of large buyers account for much of growth, so losing or reducing one has a big effect.
If many makers add capacity, prices can drop, which reduces what is left after costs.
Expansion plans run late or over budget
New factories and the proposed acquisition need approvals, equipment and skilled people, and may take longer or cost more than planned.
Government and defence orders are delayed
Public-sector customers can take a long time to approve orders and pay.
A large share of sales is abroad, so exchange-rate changes and trade rules matter more than before.
update: July 2026: sales more than doubled after a weak year, and exports passed half of sales

HFCL’s 22 July 2026 results release says revenue for April–June 2026 was more than twice that of a year earlier, and exports made up more than half of revenue, compared with about a quarter a year before. A year earlier the company had made a loss and this quarter it made a profit, so the growth percentages look very large. It reported its largest order book yet, and said the proposed aerospace purchase and an ammunition complex were still being developed. These are unaudited quarterly results, not yet fully checked by auditors. The full-year figures at the end of this page cover an earlier period.
company.question: If a company’s order book is several times last year’s revenue, will next year’s revenue be that many times higher?
company.answer: No. Orders are delivered over several years, may be delayed or changed, and revenue is counted only when goods are delivered and accepted. The order book shows booked demand, not guaranteed next-year sales.
